meaning: A heritable change associated with a cell taking up external genetic material.
example: A bacterial lineage acquires a trait after exposure to material from other cells.
importantDistinction: Griffith demonstrated transformation without identifying DNA as the active substance.
whatItDoes: A bacterial lineage acquires a trait after exposure to material from other cells.
feature: A bacterial lineage acquires a trait after exposure to material from other cells.
confusion: Griffith demonstrated transformation without identifying DNA as the active substance.

meaning: Material that stores and transmits inherited biological information.
example: DNA carries genetic information in the cellular systems studied here.
importantDistinction: A molecule’s presence in a cell is not sufficient evidence that it carries heredity.
whatItDoes: DNA carries genetic information in the cellular systems studied here.
feature: DNA carries genetic information in the cellular systems studied here.
confusion: A molecule’s presence in a cell is not sufficient evidence that it carries heredity.

meaning: A detectable radioactive label used to follow the movement of material.
example: Different labels followed phage DNA and protein in separate preparations.
importantDistinction: A tracer follows the labelled material, not every molecule in the mixture.
whatItDoes: Different labels followed phage DNA and protein in separate preparations.
feature: Different labels followed phage DNA and protein in separate preparations.
confusion: A tracer follows the labelled material, not every molecule in the mixture.

meaning: A comparison designed to distinguish explanations by changing a relevant factor while keeping others comparable.
example: DNA-destroying treatment is compared with other treatments of a transforming preparation.
importantDistinction: The interpretation depends on what was changed and what was measured.
whatItDoes: DNA-destroying treatment is compared with other treatments of a transforming preparation.
feature: DNA-destroying treatment is compared with other treatments of a transforming preparation.
confusion: The interpretation depends on what was changed and what was measured.

meaning: A nucleic-acid subunit containing a sugar, phosphate and nitrogenous base.
example: A DNA nucleotide contains deoxyribose, phosphate and one of A, T, C or G.
importantDistinction: A base is one component of a nucleotide, not the whole nucleotide.
whatItDoes: A DNA nucleotide contains deoxyribose, phosphate and one of A, T, C or G.
feature: A DNA nucleotide contains deoxyribose, phosphate and one of A, T, C or G.
confusion: A base is one component of a nucleotide, not the whole nucleotide.

meaning: Specific pairing of bases across nucleic-acid strands.
example: In double-stranded DNA, A pairs with T and C with G.
importantDistinction: The paired strands are complementary, not identical sequences in the same direction.
whatItDoes: In double-stranded DNA, A pairs with T and C with G.
feature: In double-stranded DNA, A pairs with T and C with G.
confusion: The paired strands are complementary, not identical sequences in the same direction.

meaning: Oriented in opposite directions.
example: One aligned DNA strand runs 5′ to 3′ while its partner runs 3′ to 5′.
importantDistinction: Read the direction labels before copying a displayed sequence.
whatItDoes: One aligned DNA strand runs 5′ to 3′ while its partner runs 3′ to 5′.
feature: One aligned DNA strand runs 5′ to 3′ while its partner runs 3′ to 5′.
confusion: Read the direction labels before copying a displayed sequence.

meaning: The equality of A with T and C with G in standard double-stranded DNA.
example: If A is 30% of a double-stranded sample, T is also 30%.
importantDistinction: A plus T need not equal C plus G.
whatItDoes: If A is 30% of a double-stranded sample, T is also 30%.
feature: If A is 30% of a double-stranded sample, T is also 30%.
confusion: A plus T need not equal C plus G.

meaning: Replication producing DNA molecules with one parental strand and one newly synthesized strand.
example: After one replication, both daughter molecules contain an old strand paired with a new strand.
importantDistinction: The original strands are retained in separate daughter molecules.
whatItDoes: After one replication, both daughter molecules contain an old strand paired with a new strand.
feature: After one replication, both daughter molecules contain an old strand paired with a new strand.
confusion: The original strands are retained in separate daughter molecules.

meaning: An enzyme that extends a new DNA strand by adding nucleotides to its 3′ end.
example: Complementary nucleotides extend a primed strand in the 5′ to 3′ direction.
importantDistinction: It synthesizes 5′ to 3′ while reading an antiparallel template.
whatItDoes: Complementary nucleotides extend a primed strand in the 5′ to 3′ direction.
feature: Complementary nucleotides extend a primed strand in the 5′ to 3′ direction.
confusion: It synthesizes 5′ to 3′ while reading an antiparallel template.

meaning: A short newly synthesized DNA segment on the lagging strand.
example: Several fragments are made as new lagging-strand template becomes exposed.
importantDistinction: Each fragment is still synthesized 5′ to 3′.
whatItDoes: Several fragments are made as new lagging-strand template becomes exposed.
feature: Several fragments are made as new lagging-strand template becomes exposed.
confusion: Each fragment is still synthesized 5′ to 3′.

meaning: An enzyme that seals breaks in the sugar-phosphate backbone.
example: It joins adjacent DNA segments after primer replacement.
importantDistinction: Ligase seals backbone connections; helicase separates paired strands.
whatItDoes: It joins adjacent DNA segments after primer replacement.
feature: It joins adjacent DNA segments after primer replacement.
confusion: Ligase seals backbone connections; helicase separates paired strands.

meaning: The use of genetic information to produce a functional RNA or protein product.
example: A cell produces a particular protein by transcribing and translating the relevant gene.
importantDistinction: Not every gene is expressed equally in every cell.
whatItDoes: A cell produces a particular protein by transcribing and translating the relevant gene.
feature: A cell produces a particular protein by transcribing and translating the relevant gene.
confusion: Not every gene is expressed equally in every cell.

meaning: RNA that carries a sequence used to direct protein synthesis.
example: A processed mRNA moves from the nucleus to a ribosome.
importantDistinction: It carries a working copy; the DNA molecule need not leave the nucleus.
whatItDoes: A processed mRNA moves from the nucleus to a ribosome.
feature: A processed mRNA moves from the nucleus to a ribosome.
confusion: It carries a working copy; the DNA molecule need not leave the nucleus.

meaning: RNA that helps match an mRNA codon with its corresponding amino acid.
example: A charged tRNA pairs its anticodon with a codon at the ribosome.
importantDistinction: The amino acid is attached to tRNA, not directly specified by a DNA molecule at the ribosome.
whatItDoes: A charged tRNA pairs its anticodon with a codon at the ribosome.
feature: A charged tRNA pairs its anticodon with a codon at the ribosome.
confusion: The amino acid is attached to tRNA, not directly specified by a DNA molecule at the ribosome.

meaning: RNA that forms structural and catalytic parts of ribosomes.
example: Ribosomal RNA contributes to the machinery that links amino acids.
importantDistinction: Ribosomes also contain proteins.
whatItDoes: Ribosomal RNA contributes to the machinery that links amino acids.
feature: Ribosomal RNA contributes to the machinery that links amino acids.
confusion: Ribosomes also contain proteins.

meaning: The DNA strand read by RNA polymerase to construct complementary RNA.
example: A 3′-TAC-5′ template segment produces 5′-AUG-3′ RNA.
importantDistinction: It is complementary to the RNA, rather than matching its sequence.
whatItDoes: A 3′-TAC-5′ template segment produces 5′-AUG-3′ RNA.
feature: A 3′-TAC-5′ template segment produces 5′-AUG-3′ RNA.
confusion: It is complementary to the RNA, rather than matching its sequence.

meaning: The DNA strand whose 5′ to 3′ sequence matches the RNA sequence apart from T versus U.
example: Coding DNA 5′-ATG-3′ corresponds to mRNA 5′-AUG-3′.
importantDistinction: It is not the strand read as the template for that transcript.
whatItDoes: Coding DNA 5′-ATG-3′ corresponds to mRNA 5′-AUG-3′.
feature: Coding DNA 5′-ATG-3′ corresponds to mRNA 5′-AUG-3′.
confusion: It is not the strand read as the template for that transcript.

meaning: An enzyme that synthesizes RNA using a DNA template.
example: It reads the template 3′ to 5′ while extending RNA 5′ to 3′.
importantDistinction: Transcription uses RNA nucleotides and does not require Okazaki fragments.
whatItDoes: It reads the template 3′ to 5′ while extending RNA 5′ to 3′.
feature: It reads the template 3′ to 5′ while extending RNA 5′ to 3′.
confusion: Transcription uses RNA nucleotides and does not require Okazaki fragments.

meaning: Removal of introns and joining of retained exon sequences in a pre-mRNA.
example: A eukaryotic precursor is processed before mature mRNA is exported.
importantDistinction: Retained exon sequence can include untranslated regions as well as coding regions.
whatItDoes: A eukaryotic precursor is processed before mature mRNA is exported.
feature: A eukaryotic precursor is processed before mature mRNA is exported.
confusion: Retained exon sequence can include untranslated regions as well as coding regions.

meaning: A three-nucleotide sequence in mRNA interpreted during translation.
example: AUG specifies methionine and commonly serves as a start codon.
importantDistinction: Use mRNA 5′ to 3′ to consult a codon table.
whatItDoes: AUG specifies methionine and commonly serves as a start codon.
feature: AUG specifies methionine and commonly serves as a start codon.
confusion: Use mRNA 5′ to 3′ to consult a codon table.

meaning: A tRNA triplet that pairs antiparallel with an mRNA codon.
example: 3′-UAC-5′ pairs with mRNA 5′-AUG-3′.
importantDistinction: A codon table is organized by mRNA codons, not by anticodons.
whatItDoes: 3′-UAC-5′ pairs with mRNA 5′-AUG-3′.
feature: 3′-UAC-5′ pairs with mRNA 5′-AUG-3′.
confusion: A codon table is organized by mRNA codons, not by anticodons.

meaning: The grouping of a nucleotide sequence into successive triplets for translation.
example: Beginning at a different position changes which bases form each codon.
importantDistinction: The position of the start establishes which triplets are read.
whatItDoes: Beginning at a different position changes which bases form each codon.
feature: Beginning at a different position changes which bases form each codon.
confusion: The position of the start establishes which triplets are read.

meaning: An mRNA codon signalling termination rather than an amino acid.
example: UAA, UAG and UGA are standard stop signals.
importantDistinction: Stop is not an additional amino acid in the chain.
whatItDoes: UAA, UAG and UGA are standard stop signals.
feature: UAA, UAG and UGA are standard stop signals.
confusion: Stop is not an additional amino acid in the chain.

meaning: The complementary strand reported in the opposite displayed order so that it is written 5′ to 3′.
example: Template DNA supplied 5′ to 3′ must be read from its other end to construct 5′ to 3′ RNA.
importantDistinction: Complementing letters without tracking direction can reverse the message.
whatItDoes: Template DNA supplied 5′ to 3′ must be read from its other end to construct 5′ to 3′ RNA.
feature: Template DNA supplied 5′ to 3′ must be read from its other end to construct 5′ to 3′ RNA.
confusion: Complementing letters without tracking direction can reverse the message.

meaning: The ordered amino acids in a peptide or protein.
example: Met–Lys–Gly describes three residues in order.
importantDistinction: It uses amino-acid names rather than 5′ and 3′ nucleotide ends.
whatItDoes: Met–Lys–Gly describes three residues in order.
feature: Met–Lys–Gly describes three residues in order.
confusion: It uses amino-acid names rather than 5′ and 3′ nucleotide ends.

meaning: A sequence region interpreted as codons in a specified reading frame.
example: An internal coding fragment can be translated in its given frame without a start codon.
importantDistinction: A practice fragment must state whether it is a complete message or an internal segment.
whatItDoes: An internal coding fragment can be translated in its given frame without a start codon.
feature: An internal coding fragment can be translated in its given frame without a start codon.
confusion: A practice fragment must state whether it is a complete message or an internal segment.

meaning: Checking molecule identity, direction, pairing and code interpretation against explicit rules.
example: A reported RNA uses U rather than T and yields the stated peptide.
importantDistinction: A plausible-looking sequence still needs a base-by-base check.
whatItDoes: A reported RNA uses U rather than T and yields the stated peptide.
feature: A reported RNA uses U rather than T and yields the stated peptide.
confusion: A plausible-looking sequence still needs a base-by-base check.

meaning: A persistent change in a DNA sequence.
example: A DNA base substitution remains after replication and repair.
importantDistinction: An error in one RNA or protein molecule is not automatically a DNA mutation.
whatItDoes: A DNA base substitution remains after replication and repair.
feature: A DNA base substitution remains after replication and repair.
confusion: An error in one RNA or protein molecule is not automatically a DNA mutation.

meaning: A coding substitution that leaves the specified amino acid unchanged.
example: mRNA UUA changing to UUG can still specify leucine.
importantDistinction: Its classification concerns the specified coding effect, not a guarantee that every biological effect is absent.
whatItDoes: mRNA UUA changing to UUG can still specify leucine.
feature: mRNA UUA changing to UUG can still specify leucine.
confusion: Its classification concerns the specified coding effect, not a guarantee that every biological effect is absent.

meaning: A coding change that introduces a premature stop codon.
example: A translated UAU codon becomes UAA.
importantDistinction: Its effect depends on where the stop occurs and the product involved.
whatItDoes: A translated UAU codon becomes UAA.
feature: A translated UAU codon becomes UAA.
confusion: Its effect depends on where the stop occurs and the product involved.

meaning: A shift in reading frame caused by an insertion or deletion not divisible by three in a coding region.
example: Deleting one coding nucleotide changes downstream triplets.
importantDistinction: An insertion or deletion of three bases is not automatically a frameshift.
whatItDoes: Deleting one coding nucleotide changes downstream triplets.
feature: Deleting one coding nucleotide changes downstream triplets.
confusion: An insertion or deletion of three bases is not automatically a frameshift.

meaning: The production of new combinations of genetic material.
example: Crossing over creates chromosomes carrying new combinations of existing alleles.
importantDistinction: A new combination does not require every allele to be newly mutated.
whatItDoes: Crossing over creates chromosomes carrying new combinations of existing alleles.
feature: Crossing over creates chromosomes carrying new combinations of existing alleles.
confusion: A new combination does not require every allele to be newly mutated.

meaning: Transfer of genetic material between bacterial cells through direct contact.
example: A plasmid can be transferred from a donor to another bacterium.
importantDistinction: Transfer changes genetic combinations without itself producing two daughter cells.
whatItDoes: A plasmid can be transferred from a donor to another bacterium.
feature: A plasmid can be transferred from a donor to another bacterium.
confusion: Transfer changes genetic combinations without itself producing two daughter cells.

meaning: Transfer of bacterial genetic material mediated by a virus.
example: A bacteriophage carries bacterial DNA between cells.
importantDistinction: The carrier is a virus, unlike uptake of free DNA in transformation.
whatItDoes: A bacteriophage carries bacterial DNA between cells.
feature: A bacteriophage carries bacterial DNA between cells.
confusion: The carrier is a virus, unlike uptake of free DNA in transformation.

meaning: DNA located in mitochondria rather than in the nuclear chromosomes.
example: Mitochondrial sequences can be compared in studies of maternal lineages.
importantDistinction: The usual human inheritance model is predominantly maternal, and it represents only one part of ancestry.
whatItDoes: Mitochondrial sequences can be compared in studies of maternal lineages.
feature: Mitochondrial sequences can be compared in studies of maternal lineages.
confusion: The usual human inheritance model is predominantly maternal, and it represents only one part of ancestry.

meaning: A DNA molecule assembled from genetic material from different sources.
example: A plasmid carries an inserted coding sequence.
importantDistinction: Recombinant DNA describes the assembled molecule, not a guarantee of protein production.
whatItDoes: A plasmid carries an inserted coding sequence.
feature: A plasmid carries an inserted coding sequence.
confusion: Recombinant DNA describes the assembled molecule, not a guarantee of protein production.

meaning: An enzyme that cuts DNA at particular recognition sequences.
example: Matching cuts can create compatible ends on an insert and vector.
importantDistinction: Different enzymes recognize different sequences.
whatItDoes: Matching cuts can create compatible ends on an insert and vector.
feature: Matching cuts can create compatible ends on an insert and vector.
confusion: Different enzymes recognize different sequences.

meaning: A small DNA molecule used to carry an inserted sequence into a host.
example: An engineered bacterial plasmid carries a coding sequence and appropriate regulatory elements.
importantDistinction: A plasmid is not the whole bacterial chromosome.
whatItDoes: An engineered bacterial plasmid carries a coding sequence and appropriate regulatory elements.
feature: An engineered bacterial plasmid carries a coding sequence and appropriate regulatory elements.
confusion: A plasmid is not the whole bacterial chromosome.

meaning: The regulatory and cellular context that allows a gene’s product to be made.
example: A host requires suitable signals to transcribe and translate an inserted sequence.
importantDistinction: An inserted DNA sequence is not automatically expressed in every host.
whatItDoes: A host requires suitable signals to transcribe and translate an inserted sequence.
feature: A host requires suitable signals to transcribe and translate an inserted sequence.
confusion: An inserted DNA sequence is not automatically expressed in every host.

meaning: A method that amplifies a selected DNA region through repeated cycles.
example: A defined region is copied many times using primers and a heat-stable polymerase.
importantDistinction: Amplification increases copies of a selected region, not automatically every chromosome.
whatItDoes: A defined region is copied many times using primers and a heat-stable polymerase.
feature: A defined region is copied many times using primers and a heat-stable polymerase.
confusion: Amplification increases copies of a selected region, not automatically every chromosome.

meaning: Separation of molecules by movement through a gel under an electric field.
example: DNA fragments move toward the positive electrode.
importantDistinction: Fragment size affects movement through the gel.
whatItDoes: DNA fragments move toward the positive electrode.
feature: DNA fragments move toward the positive electrode.
confusion: Fragment size affects movement through the gel.

meaning: A set of DNA fragments of known sizes used as a reference in a gel.
example: A sample band is compared with reference bands to estimate fragment length.
importantDistinction: The ladder provides a size reference, not an individual’s entire genome.
whatItDoes: A sample band is compared with reference bands to estimate fragment length.
feature: A sample band is compared with reference bands to estimate fragment length.
confusion: The ladder provides a size reference, not an individual’s entire genome.

meaning: A pattern based on selected variable DNA regions used for comparison.
example: Bands or marker results are compared between samples.
importantDistinction: A compatible profile is evidence, not by itself a complete explanation of how material arrived.
whatItDoes: Bands or marker results are compared between samples.
feature: Bands or marker results are compared between samples.
confusion: A compatible profile is evidence, not by itself a complete explanation of how material arrived.

meaning: Determining the order of nucleotides in a DNA molecule.
example: A region is read to identify sequence differences.
importantDistinction: Knowing sequence does not automatically explain every functional effect.
whatItDoes: A region is read to identify sequence differences.
feature: A region is read to identify sequence differences.
confusion: Knowing sequence does not automatically explain every functional effect.

meaning: Producing genetically very similar copies of a DNA molecule, cell or organism by a specified method.
example: A DNA region is copied, or an organism develops from transferred nuclear material.
importantDistinction: Cloning DNA and cloning an entire organism are different tasks.
whatItDoes: A DNA region is copied, or an organism develops from transferred nuclear material.
feature: A DNA region is copied, or an organism develops from transferred nuclear material.
confusion: Cloning DNA and cloning an entire organism are different tasks.

meaning: An intervention intended to change, replace or alter the use of genetic information.
example: A proposed approach aims to restore a missing cellular function.
importantDistinction: Delivery, target specificity and functional outcomes require testing.
whatItDoes: A proposed approach aims to restore a missing cellular function.
feature: A proposed approach aims to restore a missing cellular function.
confusion: Delivery, target specificity and functional outcomes require testing.

meaning: A boundary on what a study or observation can establish.
example: A result in cultured cells does not by itself prove whole-organism benefit.
importantDistinction: Limitations help specify the next test rather than making evidence worthless.
whatItDoes: A result in cultured cells does not by itself prove whole-organism benefit.
feature: A result in cultured cells does not by itself prove whole-organism benefit.
confusion: Limitations help specify the next test rather than making evidence worthless.
